title: Midpage Goes Native: Legal Research Inside Claude and ChatGPT, with Otto von Zastrow
author: Otto von Zastrow

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source reports Midpage’s integration with Claude and proposes examining what it means in practice, which is relevant to the cluster’s concern about control of lawyers’ working environments. However, it provides no assessment of workflow fit, adoption, renewal economics, performance or realized value, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Midpage just announced a new integration that allowed Anthropix Claude to connect Midpage’s legal research tools and case law.
And so I think it’s, it’s a good moment to step back and talk about what this kind of connection really means in practice.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source anticipates lawyers managing AI agents and stresses legal reliability, nuance and relationship work, aligning with the cluster’s claims about system governance and verification. However, it does not address whether automation undermines associate apprenticeship or endorse deliberate simulation, mentorship and independent practice as the response.
qs: So we really sort of have engineers are now becoming  product managers that are managing just teams of agents that are implementing various features.
You have to be sure that this brief is bulletproof.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports adjacent claims that AI can automate low-complexity text work and requires deliberate evaluation processes, but it does not address apprenticeship, associate leverage, partner succession, explicit training funding or broader career paths. It therefore provides insufficient evidence for a position on the cluster’s central expertise-pipeline proposition.
qs: But it is clearly something that involves huge amounts of reading and annotating of texts with very low, you know, low intelligence tasks that AI can probably already do better today.
So whether this is a human organization or a software and agents organization, you still have to build the processes to make everything accurate and put it into the structured format.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source only announces installation availability for Midpage in Claude and forthcoming ChatGPT support. It does not address whether legal AI’s benefits require organisational adaptation or human control, and provides no evidence about performance, employment, pricing or market effects.
qs: There you have instructions on how to install this in Claude and soon in ChatGPT and just give it a spin.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The source accepts that general-purpose model platforms are becoming major legal-work interfaces, then materially develops the cluster’s supplier–partner–rival account through Midpage’s strategy: integrate specialist legal data into those platforms while retaining differentiated legal capabilities. It also identifies platform dependence and defensibility risks, though its adoption and performance claims are primarily predictions and anecdotes rather than comparative evidence.
qs: The thing is that these general purpose platforms are adding many features very fast that you’re always playing catch up.
And I think with the chat platforms, like we can in a way coexist very nicely where there’s some things that…  is very legal specific that Claude is not doing.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Von Zastrow accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model: agents may perform first-wave research and more workflow execution, but lawyers still review consequential results because legal work demands high reliability and contextual nuance. He materially extends the synthesis with a concrete operating architecture in which general-purpose AI becomes the principal interface while specialist providers supply trusted legal data, citators and controls.
qs: Otto (43:22)  I would say it becomes a much smaller part of where you spend your time because agents are going to be doing the groundwork, which is often the legal research, at least the first wave of it.
You have to be sure that this brief is bulletproof.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Von Zastrow supports the cluster’s core view that AI will perform a growing share of legal production while lawyers retain important roles. His emphasis on relationship management, nuance and the need for legal outputs to be reliable before use aligns especially with bounded, human-supervised automation rather than autonomous delivery. The source does not materially address the cluster’s pricing or provider-reallocation claims.
qs: There will be some of that and that portion will increase every year over the next couple of years.
There’s a lot more nuance in the law where you can’t just test things before releasing them in the law, right?

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s account of an expanding market that benefits from structured market intelligence: it characterises legal tech as increasingly global and describes geographic directory filtering and planned regional coverage. It does not assess disciplined procurement in depth or provide evidence on product performance, adoption or revenue.
qs: But as we all know, the legal tech market is global and it’s becoming more so by the day.
In the meantime, if you are playing around in our directory, there is a way to sort it by the region served.

kp.k: Software commoditisation shifts competitive value toward data and relationships
kp.d: Von Zastrow argues that easier software creation reduces the value of a fixed software product without eliminating software itself. He distinguishes publishers' data, proprietary secondary publications, customer trust and relationships from their interfaces, predicting that these assets will remain important even as agents automate collection and processing.
qs: if you just look at a fixed piece of software, the value of that will go down because it’d be so cheap and easy to recreate from scratch within days.
software is obviously not going away, but it’s the value shifts to other parts.
they have a lot of secondary publications that are really important to niche fields and those are gonna continue to relying on it, whether it’s humans or agents.

kp.k: Connected interfaces could weaken systems of record
kp.d: Von Zastrow argues that document management, case management and other systems retain switching barriers but become vulnerable when another interface can access their contents. He distinguishes law-firm or corporate ownership of underlying information from vendor control of systems, and says major legal publishers rarely function as systems of record.
qs: then suddenly the system of record is actually very vulnerable to being taken over by a different interface.
And sometimes the data belongs to the law firms or belongs to the big corporates.
And I think if you look at the big publishers like TR and Lexis, they are actually rarely acting as a system of record at all.

kp.k: Automated data organisation expands legal knowledge-management opportunities
kp.d: Von Zastrow describes Midpage as operating hundreds of court scrapers and downloading new cases multiple times daily, with much ingestion and organisation performed through code rather than AI. He claims restructuring messy digital information is now a hundred times easier, while qualifying that uncaptured information and firms' willingness to adopt new processes remain constraints. He anticipates vendors and forward-deployed legal engineers organising firm knowledge for both lawyers and agents.
qs: We collect data from all the courts, ⁓ meaning we have hundreds of web scrapers and we download new cases from the courts multiple times per day.
AI is not even that heavily involved in this.
I’m sure there are some business processes that are just not being captured digitally anywhere, then it’s going to be difficult.
And I think that some of the vendors are going out to the law firms and using forward deployed legal engineers to now help them do these things, right? Help them make messy things organized.

kp.k: Citation processing becomes feasible for smaller vendors
kp.d: Responding to Lambert's questions about legal hierarchy, overruled cases and accuracy, von Zastrow claims AI can probably already outperform humans at high-volume reading and annotation. He presents Midpage's work as evidence that structured legal-data production no longer requires a billion-revenue company, but stresses the need to build evaluation capacity and accuracy processes. These are vendor assertions rather than independently demonstrated comparative findings.
qs: But it is clearly something that involves huge amounts of reading and annotating of texts with very low, you know, low intelligence tasks that AI can probably already do better today.
So whether this is a human organization or a software and agents organization, you still have to build the processes to make everything accurate and put it into the structured format.
But yes, it is now doable for a small company and it used to require a company that had billions in revenue.

kp.k: General-purpose AI and specialist legal tools may coexist
kp.d: Von Zastrow predicts that most firms will deploy a general-purpose enterprise chat tool alongside several legal technologies. He expects overlapping competition for lawyers' attention, while suggesting specialist vendors such as Harvey may initially implement law-firm access controls and processes better. He nevertheless expects general-purpose platforms to reach far more legal users, including transactional lawyers with occasional research questions and smaller firms.
qs: most law firms in the future will have both a general purpose chat tool like Claude or ChatyBT rolled out enterprise-wide and they will have several legal tech companies.
Harvey is going to be much better at implementing the right processes and controls from making sure access is handled in exactly the right way, because it is really understand how law firms operate.
You want fewer tools, not more tools.

kp.k: Midpage pursues distribution within general-purpose AI platforms
kp.d: Von Zastrow explains the integration strategy as reaching users already working in general-purpose chat interfaces and reducing copying between tools. He says Midpage is integrating legal data into these platforms while retaining specialised capabilities. At the interview, Claude could automatically invoke Midpage for relevant legal questions after enterprise enablement; the demonstrated ChatGPT version was not fully released. His guesses about platform audience sizes are explicitly uncertain, not measured adoption evidence.
qs: we actually have heard many of our users that they’re using Claude at the same time as they’re using the page.
The thing is that these general purpose platforms are adding many features very fast that you’re always playing catch up.
That’s just because the chat.tpt version is just not fully released yet.
But in Claude, you just ask a legal question. if it’s the type of question that you can answer with case law, then it will automatically switch and use it.

kp.k: Integrated agents perform iterative research with inspectable sources
kp.d: In a ChatGPT demonstration concerning non-competes lasting over five years, von Zastrow describes searching Midpage's case-law database rather than Google and returning citations and links to cases. He describes agents conducting five or 10 searches, opening cases and following cited authorities. Source access enables human verification of retrieved cases; the demonstration does not establish overall legal accuracy or eliminate the need to check interpretations and authority.
qs: can you find a non-compete case where the duration of a non-compete was over five years?
it’s going to search our entire database of case law ⁓ and come back with links, with citations.
And the agent is not just doing one search. It’s often doing, you know, five, 10 searches.
then opens these, finds more cases that are being mentioned.

kp.k: Desktop agents connect matter files, drafting and legal research
kp.d: Von Zastrow describes Claude Cowork accessing authorised local folders, reading hundreds of PDFs and creating or editing Word documents over tasks lasting 30 or 60 minutes. Combined with Midpage, he envisages relating discovery materials, transcripts and docket information to case law. Both hosts insist on IT permission; von Zastrow acknowledges early bugs and predicts smaller firms will obtain permission sooner.
qs: Claude can now actually edit Word documents, you know, create new ones. It can read hundreds of PDFs and it can do that all over tasks that can span, you know, 30 minutes, 60 minutes.
You might have to ask your IT for security first
you will have to ask IT
then of course you can ask how the things that it finds in your folder are related to case law.

kp.k: Agent spending may rise alongside staffing and pricing changes
kp.d: Von Zastrow reports approximately $8,000 monthly spending on developer coding tools, up from $100 monthly a year earlier, characterised as 80x growth. He conditionally projects AI developer costs exceeding human developer costs within a year if that growth continues and expects analogous legal spending increases. Separately, he relays one user's account of drafting 20-page briefs and research replacing work previously done by three people, with two people let go and more fixed-fee business. This is a vendor-carried customer anecdote, not representative labour-market evidence.
qs: We’re now spending probably, I think, around $8,000 per month just on the developers that are using coding tools to help them
We started at 100 a month just a year ago. So that’s 80x in one year.
If the growth with developer costs continues, then in a year we’d be at much more AI developer cost than human developer cost.
He actually, in this case, let go of two other people.
They also, that same person was just doing a lot more business than before on a fixed fee rather than an hourly.

kp.k: Platform dependence creates continuing competitive exposure
kp.d: Asked whether model providers could copy vendors' offerings, von Zastrow acknowledges dependence on chat platforms. His mitigation is using multiple platforms, taking advantage of currently easy switching, and concentrating on specialised problems that broad platforms will not all pursue. He also says Midpage sometimes builds features it expects platforms eventually to supply because customers need them sooner; he does not claim protection from platform competition.
qs: you’re always dependent on a platform if you sell through that.
And we are gonna be dependent on the chat platforms. We’re gonna be using multiple different ones.
is this feature something that Claude is going to have in two months or do we build it ourselves?
And sometimes we’ve even built things that we know they’re going to have eventually, but just for the next year, it’s going to be a real pain point for our users.

kp.k: Agent supervision changes work, but legal testing differs
kp.d: Drawing an analogy with coding, von Zastrow estimates that in most young companies probably 90% of code is AI-written, usually reviewed by humans but sometimes checked through tests alone. He anticipates some lawyers similarly managing agents, while stressing that relationship management, legal nuance and the inability to release a brief and fix it later make the timetable different. Asked about liability for self-built tools, he does not assign legal responsibility, instead advocating professional deployment, change management and internal evaluation.
qs: most code is probably 90 % of the code is entirely written by AI and usually the humans still review it.
Sometimes they just run a bunch of tests without reading the code specifically.
You have to be sure that this brief is bulletproof. You can’t just find out later and fix it.
But then there’ll be like change management, there’ll be internal evaluation.

kp.k: Citator reliability remains difficult and comparisons are provisional
kp.d: Gebauer frames the citator as an ultimate moat and mentions engagement with Vanderbilt Law School for an independent audit; von Zastrow rejects the ultimate-moat framing. He stresses the complexity of inter-case relationships and users' difficulty independently verifying treatment. He describes Midpage as better than Bloomberg and vLex but not always as good as Lexis and Westlaw, giving tentative figures of 90% for the latter and 89 or 86 percent for Midpage. No metric, sample, methodology or completed audit findings accompany those estimates. He anticipates more academic comparisons and context-specific citators.
qs: It’s definitely not the ultimate mode. It’s one of the more hairy problems that we had to deal with.
you have to have this big graph of how is each case related to each other case.
it’s hard to do all the verification yourself.
As far as we know so far, it is much, much better than the one of Bloomberg and Vlex and is not always as good as the one from Lexis and Westlaw.
They are at 90%.
89 or 86 percent or something like that

kp.k: Incumbents could adapt through acquisitions, automation and distribution
kp.d: Von Zastrow does not accept a simple opposition between incumbent walled gardens and Midpage's open integrations. He speculates that incumbents could acquire replacement flagship products, distribute content more widely and automate manual work. He also envisages acquisitions for durable customer relationships followed by software replacement and possible staff reductions. He acknowledges that Midpage currently covers only the U.S., unlike incumbents with multinational coverage, while suggesting software-based expansion could be faster.
qs: they might just switch out their flagship product with a different flagship product by built by someone else.
customer relations and contracts are so much more long lasting.
they have many, many countries in all of the world and we only have the U.S.
But I think that they have such a strong position with customers all over the world that they will find ways to leverage that.

kp.k: Research shifts toward assigning work and reviewing results
kp.d: Answering the hosts' three-to-five-year outlook question, von Zastrow predicts that standalone legal-research websites will occupy much less lawyer screen time rather than necessarily disappear. Agents would perform groundwork, particularly initial research, while lawyers interact with collected results and conduct follow-ups. This is a prospective workflow claim, not a demonstrated forecast of employment or complete lawyer substitution.
qs: I would say it becomes a much smaller part of where you spend your time because agents are going to be doing the groundwork, which is often the legal research, at least the first wave of it.
And so you’ll be talking to the results that AI has collected and doing some follow-ups.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Otto von Zastrow predicts that AI will shift legal technology's value away from standalone software interfaces toward data, integrations and customer relationships, while agents take over more research, document work and data organisation.
pts.d: At 03:38–06:49, von Zastrow argues that cheaply reproducible software loses value even as software use expands; connected general-purpose AI interfaces can displace the interface of a document or case management system without replacing its underlying data. At 08:29–14:43, he claims that software and AI make organising messy legal data dramatically easier and enable small companies to undertake case annotation and citation-treatment work previously requiring very large publishers. He predicts more accurate, consistent organisation of law-firm knowledge, accessible to both lawyers and agents. He nevertheless expects established publishers to survive, partly because of proprietary secondary publications. At 15:02–19:59, he predicts coexistence between enterprise-wide general-purpose chat tools and specialist legal tools, but expects general-purpose platforms to attract vastly more legal users overall. He presents Midpage's integrations as combining general-purpose models with legal data and claims this combination can outperform earlier CoCounsel or Lexis+ AI offerings. In his account, standalone vendor websites become less valuable as agents access specialised capabilities through integrations. At 20:13–21:20, he predicts rapidly rising spending on agents and reports one user's substitution of AI-assisted work for two employees alongside increased fixed-fee business. At 25:42–27:24 and 29:28–31:39, he describes agents reading large document collections, editing Word files, connecting matter documents to case law and conducting iterative searches with follow-up exploration of cited cases. At 33:49–36:25, he predicts that some lawyers will increasingly direct agents rather than produce all work themselves, while professional software builders remain important despite easier internal tool creation. At 37:00–38:31, he predicts future citators will identify negative treatment relevant to the user's particular matter, rather than merely flagging treatment generally. At 39:24–40:45, he suggests incumbents may acquire businesses for customers, replace their software, automate editorial operations and distribute content more widely. At 43:22–43:49, he predicts that standalone research websites will occupy much less lawyer time as agents conduct initial research and lawyers work with the results and follow-ups, rather than asserting that research platforms disappear entirely.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are supported chiefly by von Zastrow's experience operating Midpage, a product demonstration, informal comparative estimates and a single customer anecdote; most market-wide predictions are not accompanied by systematic evidence.
pts.d: For data automation, von Zastrow describes Midpage operating hundreds of court scrapers, downloading cases multiple times daily and organising content through substantial conventional code as well as some AI. His claim that transforming unstructured data is 'a hundred times easier' is not supported by a measured comparison in the transcript. His descriptions of publishers' manual editorial processes and AI's potential superiority are offered as explanations, not as documented comparative studies. For increasing agent expenditure, he reports Midpage's developer coding-tool spending rising from $100 monthly a year earlier to approximately $8,000 monthly, an 80-fold increase, and extrapolates from this to legal work. For labour and pricing effects, he recounts a conversation with one user on the preceding Tuesday: AI-assisted research and 20-page briefs reportedly replaced work formerly done by three people, two people were let go, and the user was doing more fixed-fee business. This is a customer anecdote, not a sector-wide employment finding. For integrated research, he demonstrates a ChatGPT/Midpage search for a non-compete case involving a duration over five years, describing returned citations and links to underlying cases. He presents those links as enabling human verification; the demonstration does not establish comprehensive accuracy or absence of hallucination in generated answers. For citator quality, he offers approximate figures of 90% for Lexis and Westlaw and 86% or 89% for Midpage, while claiming Midpage is substantially better than Bloomberg and vLex. He gives no metric definition, sample, protocol or published results in the transcript. His own statement is that further academic comparative reporting is planned; the host's reference to a Vanderbilt audit is not itself evidence supplied by him of completed independent findings. His estimates of Claude's audience and legal-user numbers are explicitly tentative. The broader predictions about interface migration, firm adoption, acquisitions, and agent-directed legal practice rest on commercial experience, analogies with smartphone apps and coding, and expectations rather than cited studies.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Von Zastrow distinguishes claimed present capabilities from near-term product expansion and longer-term workflow changes, with adoption, permissions, data availability and accuracy processes as important qualifications.
pts.d: He presents inexpensive software creation, data transformation and some automated annotation as already possible, while qualifying the latter as work AI can 'probably' do better today. Data organisation depends on the relevant information being digitally captured; technical feasibility does not ensure that firms will accept a new process or data structure. Accurate legal datasets still require deliberate evaluation and quality processes. His forecasts of general-purpose chat adoption and incumbent adaptation mostly have no fixed date; he expects large enterprises to take a long time to accumulate many integrated apps and specialist legal vendors initially to handle firm-specific access controls better. At the interview date, he describes the Claude integration as usable but the ChatGPT version as not fully released, with broader integration into chat-enabled tools coming 'very soon'. Desktop access to matter files requires security permission, and enterprise use of the plugin requires IT enablement. He acknowledges bugs in the newly released Cowork product, although he predicts these are temporary. His forecast that AI developer costs could exceed human developer costs within a year is explicitly conditional on continued spending growth; the comparable rise in lawyers' agent spending is an extrapolation without a precise deadline. He expects agent-direction aspects of legal work to increase annually over the next few years but says legal work will follow a different timetable from coding because legal outputs cannot be tested and repaired after release in the same way and require more relational and contextual judgment. The final reduction in time spent on standalone research websites is his answer to a three-to-five-year question. He treats citator quality as a moving target and context-specific citators as a future possibility. His optimism about platform dependence is conditional on continued competition and easy switching, and he acknowledges that platforms may absorb features vendors currently supply. Midpage's dataset is described as US-only at present, with possible faster future geographic expansion rather than a claim of current worldwide coverage.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect lawyers' workflows, smaller firms' adoption, large firms' knowledge and access controls, legal-data vendors' business models, publishers' competitive advantages and some legal and software jobs.
pts.d: Litigators are expected to delegate first-wave research, analyse large discovery collections and dockets, develop briefs and review linked authorities through conversational interfaces. Transactional lawyers and corporate legal users with occasional enforceability questions are expected to use familiar general-purpose chat tools instead of opening specialist research websites. Smaller firms are identified as likely early adopters of desktop agents because permissions can be obtained sooner and a general-purpose tool with document integrations may cover many needs. Large firms are expected to retain both general-purpose and specialist AI tools, invest in organising internal knowledge and require appropriate access controls and IT approval. Lawyers remain involved in reviewing research results and legal outputs; von Zastrow does not predict uniform unsupervised substitution or universal job losses. His one reported customer combined staff reductions with greater fixed-fee output, while he says increased workload rather than dismissal often follows. Legal-tech vendors face pressure on standalone interfaces and easily replicated features, opportunities in specialised data and integration, and dependence on general-purpose platforms. Midpage is positioned as a legal-data and research-tool vendor, not a provider delivering legal work outside the law-firm form. Forward-deployed legal engineers are described as helping firms organise data. Incumbent publishers retain proprietary secondary content, customer trust, contracts and global distribution, while facing automation of editorial work and possible software replacement through acquisitions. Potentially displaced workers include personnel maintaining acquired software and legal-publishing annotation operations, although the interview provides no aggregate employment estimate. In the coding comparison, developers increasingly manage agents, with spending shifting toward AI tools. No concrete claim is made about closing the civil justice gap.
